analysis.one_liner: Narrows FDA approval of controlled-release oxycodone to severe-only pain.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee and died there at the end of the Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ordered the Food and Drug Administration to change the approved labeling of controlled-release oxycodone, the opioid sold as OxyContin, so the drug could be marketed only for severe pain rather than for moderate-to-severe pain. Backers argued the broader label let the drug be prescribed for millions of milder pain cases, fueling addiction and abuse. The bill sat in committee without a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and communities at risk of opioid addiction and overdose, because a narrower label would sharply shrink the pool of people for whom the drug can be lawfully prescribed and marketed. It would also direct the FDA to keep future versions of the drug to the narrower use.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the FDA Commissioner, within 90 days, to modify the approval of any drug containing controlled-release oxycodone to limit its approved use to severe-only pain instead of moderate-to-severe pain, and to limit any later approval the same way [S2] [S3].
The change applies to drugs entering interstate commerce starting 180 days after enactment, so the narrower label would take effect quickly [S3].

Narrowing the approved label reduces the number of prescriptions that can be legally written for milder pain, which is the pathway backers identified for abuse and addiction of this long-acting opioid [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The manufacturers of controlled-release oxycodone, above all the maker of OxyContin, would lose a large share of the market, since moderate-pain prescribing would no longer be within the approved label. Patients with moderate chronic pain who relied on the drug could lose access to it as prescriptions fell outside the label.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oxycodone manufacturers and some pain patients

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the drug's approved use for moderate pain, so patients whose doctors judged the drug appropriate for moderate chronic pain could lose access to it [S2] [S3].

Restricting the label is a blunt instrument compared with abuse-deterrent formulations, prescribing guidelines, and enforcement tools, and it does nothing to stop diversion of the drug once prescribed for severe pain; it is a one-time labeling mandate rather than a broader addiction-treatment strategy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed at one of the main engines of the opioid epidemic: a long-acting opioid approved for everyday moderate pain, which produced a huge prescribing base and a large diverted supply. The cost falls on the manufacturer's revenue and on a smaller group of moderate-pain patients, some of whom would need alternative treatment. The tradeoff is real but the public-health upside was the clear aim of the bill's bipartisan sponsors.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 21, 2013, by Rep. Stephen Lynch with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, and was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which took no further action; the committee never reported the bill to the House floor [S5].
The bill had 8 cosponsors split evenly between Republicans and Democrats, yet no action followed beyond the two referrals during the two-year Congress [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The makers of controlled-release oxycodone, led by the maker of OxyContin, are better off: the broader moderate-to-severe pain label that underpins their sales was never touched, and no restrictions were imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: OxyContin's maker kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Stephen Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the FDA to limit controlled-release oxycodone to severe-only pain.

for.name: 8 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors (4 Republicans, 4 Democrats, including Reps. Fitzpatrick, Hal Rogers of Kentucky, Rahall, Keating, Wolf, and Slaughter as original cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support before it went to committee.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill by referral and never scheduled action on it; it was never reported to the House floor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from March 2013 until the Congress ended without a hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's cosponsors split evenly, 4 Republicans and 4 Democrats, so its death in committee was not a party-line defeat but the result of no action in a committee controlled by the majority.

industries.industry: Makers of controlled-release oxycodone (Purdue Pharma's OxyContin and generic versions)
industries.note: The bill would have forced the FDA to narrow the drug's approved use from moderate-to-severe pain to severe-only pain within months, shrinking the legal prescribing market that generated the drug's sales. Its interest in keeping the broad label ran against the public's interest in fewer opioid prescriptions and less diversion.
